title: Cargo hold hatch covers
plain: Do officers know the hatch cover procedures, and are the hatch covers gas tight and in good condition?
why: On an OBO, a leaking hatch cover lets gas or oil escape onto the deck or into the holds.
checks: Company procedure for operating, inspecting, maintaining and testing hatch covers
Inspection and maintenance records
Sealing arrangements, P/V valves and hydraulic system on the covers
Hatch coaming corners and deck nearby for cracks or grab damage
Risk assessment for any gas or liquid leak
ready: Hatch cover procedure and maker's manual
Hatch covers in the planned maintenance system
Record of inert gas pressure test of the seals before liquid cargo
Record of seal check after loading
Risk assessments for any leak that could not be stopped
traps: Seals not dual seal type; hatch covers missing from the maintenance plan
No pressure test with inert gas before loading liquid cargo
Ongoing leak at seals or P/V valve flanges
Leak with no risk assessment
Oil leaking from hydraulics, cracks at coaming corners, unrepaired grab damage
Officer does not know the best tank pressure range for a good seal
say: Our SMS covers operation, inspection, testing and maintenance of the hatch covers, and they are in our maintenance plan. Before loading liquid cargo we pressure test the seals with inert gas and record it. After loading we check the seals again, and any leak we cannot stop goes to risk assessment.

practice.q: How do you prove the hatch seals are tight before loading oil?
a: Apply soapy solution to the seals
Adjust closing devices where it leaks

practice.q: What do you do if a hatch cover still leaks after adjusting?
a: Plan repair of the joint at the earliest chance
Use extra sealing only as the risk assessment allows

tip: Know the tank pressure range your procedure gives for a good seal. Inspectors ask for it.

title: Changing between wet and dry cargoes
plain: Do officers know how to change cargo mode between oil and dry bulk, and are checklists and records available?
why: A wrong changeover can leave oil, gas or residues in holds, lines or sounding pipes, and cause fire, explosion or contamination.
checks: Company procedure for changing cargo mode
Ship-specific changeover checklists
Completed checklists from past changeovers
Hold inspection records and repairs after dry cargo (discharge equipment damage)
ready: Changeover procedure with oil to dry and dry to oil checklists
Completed checklists from the last changeovers
Hold inspection records before changeover
Records of corrective action after grab damage
traps: No procedure for changing mode; checklists generic, not ship-specific
Checklists not completed as required
No records of previous changeovers
Records show the procedure was not followed
No hold inspection records before changeover
Officer not familiar with the procedure
say: Our procedure covers both directions of changeover with a ship-specific checklist. We complete every item, inspect the holds and record any damage and repairs. Records of past changeovers are available for you to review.

practice.q: What are the main steps going from oil to dry cargo?
a: Wash and gas free holds and tanks
Flush and drain suctions and lines
Blank off suctions, droplines and gas lines
Check hatch seals and ballast spaces for gas

practice.q: And from dry cargo to oil?
a: Remove blanks and set up venting
Clean strainers and hatch seals, prove valves and NRVs
Inert holds and check tightness before loading

tip: Keep the changeover checklists together with the hold inspection reports so one folder tells the full story.

title: Cargo and ballast transfer planning and execution
plain: Do officers know how to plan cargo and ballast transfers, and do records show the plan was followed?
why: A poor or ignored plan leads to overfill, bad stress or trim, contamination, or spills.
checks: Company procedure for planning and recording cargo and ballast transfers
A recent plan: content, draught, trim and stress figures, signatures
Records of the same operation compared against the plan
Whether plan was updated and re-approved after any change
ready: Company procedures for planning and for record keeping
Plans and records of recent operations
Plan signed by C/O and deck officers, approved by Master, signed by terminal
Draught, trim and stress calculations for key stages
Records showing tanks, pumps and lines used at any time
traps: Plan missing key information or stress, trim and draught figures
Not signed by all officers, or not approved by Master
Sequence in records differs from the plan
Operations carried out that were not in the plan
Plan changed but not updated and re-approved
Records too thin to rebuild the operation; tank atmosphere or venting not as planned
say: We plan every cargo and ballast transfer in writing with our procedure, including stress, trim and draught checks. The Master approves it and the officers and terminal sign it. If anything changes we update the plan and get it approved again before continuing.

practice.q: What does your transfer plan contain?
a: Sequence, rates and tank atmosphere or venting method
Draught, trim and stress at key stages
Any COW, tank cleaning or gas freeing

practice.q: What if the sequence has to change during the operation?

tip: Write rate change requests and confirmations in the log so you can rebuild the operation later.

title: Ship/Shore Safety Checklist (SSSCL)
plain: Do cargo officers know the SSSCL, and is it completed and followed all through the operation?
why: The checklist is the written agreement between ship and terminal that keeps the operation safe.
checks: Company procedure requiring the SSSCL for every cargo, tank cleaning and ballast operation
Current and two earlier SSSCLs, with items picked at random for you to explain
Part 6 agreements and whether the plan reflects them
Part 8 repetitive checks and the deck check each watch
Open defects compared with SSSCL remarks
ready: Company procedure on SSSCL use
SSSCLs for current and at least two earlier operations
Cargo records and the Bridge Log Book
Evidence for any item needing documents
Open defect list matched to SSSCL remarks
traps: Relevant sections not completed or not in use
Open defect on relevant equipment not declared in SSSCL remarks
Defective equipment with no defect report and no remark
Item answered yes but ship is not in line with ISGOTT; ship breaking a Part 6 agreement
Plan not updated to match the pre-transfer agreements
No responsible officer deck check each watch, or officer cannot explain a check
say: We complete the relevant SSSCL sections for every operation and keep the agreements throughout. I can explain how each check is done and show the evidence. Any defect affecting the checklist is declared in the remarks to the terminal.

practice.q: Pick any item and show me how you check it.
a: Explain the check in your own words
Link it to the ISGOTT reference

practice.q: How often are the repetitive checks done?
a: As agreed in the pre-transfer conference
A responsible officer checks the deck at least once each watch

tip: Before the inspector picks an item, check your SSSCL answers against what is actually on deck.

title: Cargo operations team composition
plain: Do officers know the supervision level needed in cargo operations, and was the right team on duty?
why: Too few or distracted people means leaks, mooring problems or slow reaction in an emergency.
checks: Company procedure on supervision and support for cargo and port operations
Cargo plans showing manning for each stage
Team in the CCR and on deck during the inspection
Whether team members are pulled into other work (SIMOPS)
Senior officer supervision at critical stages
ready: Company procedure on cargo team and supervision
Cargo or port plans for current operation and last three months or six operations, whichever is fewer
Bridge Log Book
Plans that list manning for connecting hoses, start, bulk, topping off, COW, stripping, draining
traps: No procedure on supervision levels
Plan does not state supervision needed at each stage
Plan not in line with the procedure
Team on duty not matching the procedure
Deck watch distracted by SIMOPS or by sounding and surveying
Critical stage such as COW, start or finish of cargo without senior officer
say: Our procedure sets the minimum team and supervision for each stage of cargo work, and our plans state it. Moorings and access stay tended all the time. Critical stages like starting, topping off and COW have the senior officer present.

practice.q: Who is on duty during topping off?
a: Deck watch in contact by radio
Extra support for mooring and access
Senior officer if the procedure requires

practice.q: What if SIMOPS happens during cargo?
a: Cargo and mooring watch not distracted

tip: Check the watch list against your plan before each stage. Do not let one rating cover moorings, gangway and sounding at once.

title: Cargo and ballast valve testing
plain: Do officers know how cargo and ballast valves are tested, and are the valves and remote control in good order?
why: A valve that is slow, wrong in indication or stuck can cause surge pressure, spills or loss of control of the cargo.
checks: Company procedure with test frequency, records and valve timing
Records of actual opening and closing times
Local and remote valve indicator checks
Emergency valve control mode and local hand pump
Valves and hydraulic or pneumatic system on deck
ready: Valve test procedure and maker's manual
Ship drawings with design open and close times for each valve
Test records with actual times and indicator checks
Emergency mode and hand pump test records
Hydraulic system at normal pressure
traps: No procedure or no records of valve tests
Times not recorded, or valves outside optimum times; indicator shows wrong position
Remote valve isolated or operated manually due to hydraulic leak
Hydraulic pressure not held during transfer or no automatic pressure keeping
Excessive hydraulic oil loss
No working emergency hand pump, or officer cannot operate it
say: Our procedure sets how often we test valves, how we time them and how we check indicators, and we record the results. I know the design times for our valves, and what to do if one is out. I can also operate the emergency mode and hand pump.

practice.q: What do you do if a valve closes faster than its design time?
a: Check against ship drawings and manual
Take care for surge risk until corrected

practice.q: Show me how the emergency valve control works.

tip: Keep the design valve times in a simple table at the CCR so you can quote them quickly.

title: Fixed cargo tank level gauging system
plain: Do officers know how the fixed level gauging system is run, tested and compared, and does it work?
why: If the gauges are wrong or fail, you may not know the tank level, so overfill and spills become likely.
checks: Company procedure for operation, maintenance, testing, calibration and comparison
Test, calibration and comparison records
You demonstrating the system
What you do if a gauge fails or is unreliable
Level alarm settings
ready: Procedure and maker's manual
Maintenance, test, calibration and comparison records
Comparison checks against portable or secondary gauges
Risk assessment based procedure for continuing cargo if gauging fails
traps: No procedure based on maker's instructions
Testing and calibration not done as required or no records
No comparison checks, or big differences found
No risk assessment procedure for gauge failure
System inoperative or unreliable and portable gauges in use
Level alarms silenced or inhibited; officer unsure of failure actions or alarm settings
say: We test, calibrate and compare the fixed gauges as our procedure and the maker require, and keep records. If a gauge is unreliable we follow our risk assessed procedure to continue safely. I can show you the system and the level alarm settings.

practice.q: What do you do if one tank gauge fails during loading?
a: Follow the risk assessed company procedure
Use portable or secondary gauging as allowed
Check any replacement unit is compatible and calibrated

practice.q: How do you check the fixed gauges are accurate?
a: Compare with portable or secondary gauges
Calibrate as the maker's manual says

tip: If the ship has no fixed gauging, the guidance says to mark Not Answerable then Not Applicable. Know that your ship is truly exempt.

title: Stability and loading instruments
plain: Do deck officers know the testing procedure for the stability and loading instruments, and are test records kept?
why: If the instrument is wrong, stress and stability may be miscalculated and the ship overstressed.
checks: Company procedure for testing the instrument
Latest test using an approved test condition and maker's instructions
Test at special survey with a class surveyor present
You demonstrating the damage stability function
Instrument manual
ready: Company procedure and instruction manual
Regular test records by ship staff
Annual survey test records
Special survey test records with surveyor
Exemption certificate if no instrument is required
traps: No company procedure for periodic testing
Officer unfamiliar with testing or damage stability function
Periodic accuracy checks not done or no records
No record of test at special survey with class surveyor
Instrument defective
No instrument and no proof of exemption
say: Our procedure requires regular tests of the instrument with approved test conditions, at least at annual and special surveys. Records are kept and I can show them. I can also run the damage stability function.

practice.q: How do you test the loading instrument?
a: Use an approved test condition, not an actual loading

practice.q: Show me the damage stability function.

tip: Practise the damage stability screen before the inspection. It is a common request.

title: Loading limitations
plain: If the ship has loading or stability limits, are there company procedures and do officers know them?
why: Wrong tank filling levels or unmanaged free surface can overstress the structure or reduce stability.
checks: Loading and stability manual: any density, filling height or stability limits
Whether the limits were declared correctly in the pre-inspection questionnaire
Company procedure that warns staff and says how to avoid or reduce the problem
Cargo and ballast plans addressing the limits
Warning signs in the CCR
ready: Loading and stability manual
Company procedure on loading limits and stability concerns
Recent plans and records showing the limits were followed
Evidence the loading instrument and stability booklet were updated after scrubber, BWTS or major modification
traps: Limits not declared in the questionnaire
No company procedure to manage the limits
No warning signs posted for cargo officers
Officer unaware of the limits on the ship
Plans do not address the limits, or records show they were not followed
Weight change from scrubber or BWTS but loading instrument and booklet not updated
say: Our loading manual and company procedure tell us about the limits on this ship, such as filling heights and free surface. They are posted in the CCR and built into our cargo plans. I can show you records that we followed them.

practice.q: What loading limits or stability concerns apply to this ship?
a: Name them from the loading manual
Say which tanks or phases they apply to
Explain how the plan avoids or mitigates them

practice.q: What happens to the stability booklet if a scrubber is fitted?

tip: If your ship has no restrictions, be ready to show the manual that says so. The question is then answered N/A.

title: Cargo transfer hoses
plain: Do officers know how cargo hoses are selected, inspected, tested and stored, and are the hoses in good condition?
why: A failed or unsuitable hose means a spill or gas release at the manifold.
checks: Company procedure for selection, inspection, testing, storage and retirement
Hose markings, certificates and compatibility data
Test, elongation and electrical continuity records and service history
Hoses in use or stored on board
Your knowledge of pre-use checks and hose limits
ready: Hose procedure with retirement criteria
Certificates and compatibility data for each hose
Inspection records at least every 12 months
Hydrostatic test records at 1.5 times maximum working pressure, with elongation
Electrical continuity test since last hydrostatic test
Usage history for each hose
traps: Hose not clearly marked with required information
No inspection or pressure test in last 12 months; visual damage but hose not withdrawn
No electrical continuity test since the last pressure test
Hose not compatible with cargo or temperature, or working pressure under 1 MPa
Stored or used below minimum bend radius; poor storage, or flow rate above maker's limit
LNG hoses not tested before each use or under an alternative documented procedure
say: Our procedure covers selecting hoses for the cargo, inspecting them before every use, and testing at least yearly. Each hose has a certificate, markings and a service history. Damaged or expired hoses are withdrawn and the reason is recorded.

practice.q: What do you check before using a hose?
a: Damage, slippage or misalignment of the assembly
Cuts or abrasions through the cover

practice.q: How do you store the hoses?
a: Follow the company procedure and maker's guidance
Keep above the minimum bend radius
For cryogenic hoses: blank flanges and nitrogen charged

tip: Check the paint-stencilled test date on every hose against your records before the inspector does.

title: Cargo and ballast controls, indicators and mimics
plain: Are cargo and ballast controls and indicators checked for accuracy, and are clear up-to-date mimic or pipeline diagrams available?
why: The cargo officer makes decisions from these readings, so wrong information can lead to wrong actions.
checks: Mimic or pipeline diagrams in the CCR and pumproom: legible and up to date
Pressure, temperature, draught, list and trim readings look sensible
Pumps controlled from CCR, not locally or from the engine room
Valve and pump status on mimic matches reality
Company procedure and records for periodic sensor checks
ready: Procedure for verifying sensors and displays
Records of pressure, temperature and draught gauge checks
Updated pipeline diagrams after any modification
Open defect reports for any known fault
traps: Diagrams missing, not legible or not updated after a modification
Pipe marking does not match the mimic; no procedure or no records of sensor accuracy checks
Pump run from the engine room or deck because remote control is faulty
Pump speed or load indicator wrong or out of service
Draught gauges or pressure and temperature displays inaccurate
Mimic showing wrong valve position, level, pressure or alarm status
say: We check our pressure, temperature, level and draught sensors and the mimic displays regularly under our procedure and keep records. The pipeline diagrams are current and posted in the CCR and pumproom. Any fault we cannot fix ourselves goes into the defect report.

practice.q: How do you know the mimic shows the true valve position?
a: Periodic checks of indicators against local position

practice.q: What if a remote pump control fails?
a: Avoid normalising running pump from engine room or locally

tip: A single sensor fault that is already on an open defect report is not an observation. Keep the defect list up to date.

title: Cargo system bonding
plain: Do officers know how cargo tanks, plant and pipelines are bonded, and are the bonding arrangements in good condition?
why: Bonding stops static electricity building up and sparking in a flammable atmosphere.
checks: Company procedure for inspecting and maintaining bonding
Bonding straps on the deck, visible and in good condition
Ship drawings showing where bonding is required
Your understanding of what the bonding does
ready: Procedure, possibly in the planned maintenance system
Drawings or instruction books showing bonding as fitted
Inspection and maintenance records
traps: No company procedure
Officer unfamiliar with the ship's bonding arrangements
Required straps missing or mechanically damaged
Straps covered by paint or corrosion so they cannot be inspected or conduct poorly
Any bonding arrangement defective
say: Bonding is there to prevent static discharge between parts at different voltages. We inspect the straps under our maintenance plan, keep them clean, unpainted and undamaged, and repair or renew them to the original design.

practice.q: Where on this ship do you need bonding straps?
a: Where pipes or tanks are not fixed to the hull

practice.q: What can ruin a bonding strap?

tip: After any pipe work or painting on deck, walk the area and check every strap is back and clean.

title: Independent check of cargo line-up
plain: Is there a procedure for a second person to check the whole cargo, vapour and vent line-up before operations start?
why: One missed valve or open drain can cause a spill, cross-contamination or overpressure.
checks: Company procedure on independent cross-check: who, when, where recorded
Records of a recent operation showing the check was done
Drains, stubs, sampling points and vacuum breakers: valved, closed and capped or blanked
Your understanding of the procedure
ready: Procedure for second person cross-check
Cargo records or checklists with the check signed before start
Responsible officer sign-off for the line-up
Line-up verified against the cargo plan
traps: No procedure for independent check
No evidence it was done before starting
Drain, stub, sampling or vacuum breaker valve left open
One of those connections without a valve
Not capped or blanked where needed
Officer cannot say who does the cross-check or where it is recorded
say: Before every operation one officer sets the lines per the plan, and a second person checks the entire liquid, vapour and vent system independently. The responsible officer signs it in the cargo records. I also check that drains, sampling points and vacuum breakers are closed and capped.

practice.q: Who does the second check?
a: A person other than the one who set the lines

practice.q: What else do you check besides the main valves?
a: Drains and sampling connections closed and capped
Vacuum breakers, P/V valves and vapour lines set
Stern line isolated if not used

tip: Check again after a change of grade. When the line-up changes for a grade change, check it again in the same way.

title: Mooring winch brake testing and operation
plain: Do deck officers know how winch brakes are tested and operated, and do records show tests were done on time?
why: A brake that slips early or holds too hard can part lines or fail to protect them in surge.
checks: Company procedure for use and testing of winch brakes
Mooring System Management Plan and brake test records
Test at least annually, after maintenance, or after premature slippage
Winch markings: test date, brake load, torque or pressure setting, reeling direction
Lines reeled correctly, brake condition, brake set as marked
ready: Mooring procedure and MSMP
Line Management Plan
Brake test records, with brake set to render at 60% of ship design MBL
Calibration certificate for the test gauge if carried
Maker's instructions and maintenance records after repairs
Photo of a brake mechanism uploaded to the portal
traps: No procedure, or no MSMP in line with MEG4; officer or crew unfamiliar with setting and operating the brakes
Brakes not tested periodically, after repair or after slippage
Drum not marked with test date, brake load, reeling direction or setting
A brake set wrongly on any drum in use; locking nut stopper on the tightening screw
Line reeled in wrong direction, or more than one layer on the tension side of a split drum
Brake linings or drums defective, or drums with more than light surface rust
say: Our procedure and mooring plan set when and how the brakes are tested and adjusted to 60% of the ship design MBL. Test dates, settings and reeling direction are marked on each winch. I know the signs that a brake needs retesting, and records are available.

practice.q: What do you do if a brake slips early during mooring?
What should be marked on a winch drum?
What does the mark on the brake handle spindle mean?
a: It is the indicator for the correct brake setting
Set the brake so it lines up with the mark
A brake set off the mark is not set as required

tip: Check the marking and tags on every winch before the inspection. Missing tags are easy observations.

title: Was the vessel satisfactorily moored
plain: Is the ship moored in line with both the terminal mooring plan and the patterns allowed by our mooring plan?
why: Too few lines or bad angles can let the ship move at the berth and break lines or hoses.
checks: MSMP: optimal, sub-optimal and alternate mooring patterns
Terminal mooring plan compared with the MSMP
Actual lines: number, services, horizontal and vertical angles
Swamp lines or shore lines required by terminal are in use
Mooring analysis or double banking plan, if any
ready: MSMP showing permitted patterns and angle limits
Terminal mooring plan from handbook or standard publication
Passage plan, pilot card or cargo plan showing the layout used
Mooring analysis or double banking plan where required
traps: No MSMP in line with MEG4, or no alternate patterns shown; no maximum angle limits in the plan
Officer cannot explain how terminal plan is compared with MSMP
Pattern not following the terminal plan or the MSMP
Line vertical angle above the limit in the MSMP
Fewer lines than either plan needs, or supplementary shore lines not used
Double banked with no analysis showing both ships are restrained
say: Before berthing we compare the terminal plan with the patterns allowed in our mooring plan. Where they differ in line numbers we follow the plan needing more lines. We check line angles and use any shore lines the terminal requires.

practice.q: The terminal plan asks for 8 lines and our plan for 10. What do you use?
What if a shore hook is out of service?
a: Check alternate patterns in the MSMP

tip: If the terminal has no published plan, keep proof that you asked your operator or agent for it.

title: Line Management Plan (LMP)
plain: Do officers and mooring ratings know the Line Management Plan, and is it kept up to date with certificates for every line, tail and shackle?
why: Lines that are overused, damaged or unidentified can part in service and kill someone through snap-back.
checks: LMP follows MEG4 Table 5.2 and is easy to reach
Certificate for every line, tail and joining shackle, matched to its location
Service life, inspection history and end-for-ending records
Incident report for any line that parted in service
Lines, tails and shackles on deck: tagged, in good order, tails connected correctly
Splicing rules and who may splice
ready: Line Management Plan
Manufacturer certificates for all lines, tails and shackles, including spares
Inspection and maintenance records
Retirement criteria and elapsed time or hours in service
Incident investigation report for any line failure in last six months
Record of which tail is fitted to which line
traps: No LMP, or it does not follow MEG4 Table 5.2; certificates missing or not matched to location
Rating does not know the LMP exists or what it says for his job
LMP inaccurate: items in wrong place or not listed; inspections not done as the LMP says
Line or tail used past retirement criteria or badly damaged
Shackles fitted the wrong way round, or cow hitch or wrong shackle on a wire to tail
Splices not to maker's instructions, lines not end-for-ended; line parted in last six months with no investigation report
say: Our Line Management Plan covers maintenance, inspection, service life and retirement. Every line, tail and shackle is tagged and matched to its certificate. We inspect as the plan requires, and record any line change or failure.

practice.q: Where do you find the history of this mooring line?
a: In the LMP, by the line tag

practice.q: Can you move a line from one winch to another?

tip: Walk the deck with the LMP list in hand and check tags against it. Swapped or untagged lines are common finds.

title: Mooring lines, tails and shackles
plain: Do all lines, tails and joining shackles, including spares, meet industry strength guidelines?
why: Lines or tails too weak, or shackles too small, can fail at the load they should be able to carry.
checks: MSMP: ship design MBL and working load limit of the lines
Line design break force 100 to 105% of ship design MBL
Tail design break force 125 to 130% of ship design MBL
Joining shackle safe working load at least the line working load limit
Spot check of the equipment list against certificates
ready: Mooring System Management Plan
List of loose equipment with LDBF and TDBF
File of manufacturer certificates for all lines, tails and shackles
Nylon lines certified for wet break test
traps: No MSMP, or no certificate file for all items
Any line, in use or spare, below 100% of ship design MBL
Any tail below 125% of ship design MBL
Joining shackle with safe working load below line working load limit
Values above range may be commented on by the inspector (lines over 105%, tails over 130%)
say: Our MSMP lists ship design MBL and line working load limit. All our lines, tails and shackles, including spares, have certificates and fall within the guideline ranges. I can show you the equipment list and certificates.

practice.q: What strength should a mooring line have compared with ship design MBL?
And the tail and the shackle?
a: Tail 125 to 130% of ship design MBL
Shackle safe working load at least line working load limit

tip: Check the spares in the store too. A weak spare line is still an observation.

title: Emergency towing procedure and equipment
plain: Do officers know the ship's emergency towing booklet, and is the towing gear ready for immediate use?
why: After a breakdown, a quick and correct tow connection can stop a drifting loaded tanker grounding.
checks: Ship-specific Emergency Towing Booklet (ETB) matching the equipment fitted
Copies on the bridge, in the forecastle, and in the ship's office or CCR
Condition of emergency towing arrangements, evidence of recent maintenance
Ancillary equipment listed in the ETB is in the right place
Your knowledge of how to deploy it
ready: ETB, three copies in correct places
Emergency towing gear at both ends (tankers of 20,000 dwt and above)
Maintenance records for the towing gear
Ancillary items checked against the ETB list
traps: ETB not based on the equipment actually fitted
ETB missing from bridge, forecastle or office or CCR
Officer unfamiliar with the ETB, equipment or deployment
Towing arrangement defective or not ready for immediate use
Ancillary equipment missing, defective or in the wrong place
say: Our ship-specific Emergency Towing Booklet is on the bridge, forecastle and in the CCR. The gear is maintained and ready for immediate use. I can explain how we would deploy it step by step.

practice.q: Where are the ETB copies kept?
How would you rig the emergency towing arrangement?
a: Follow the ETB for our equipment
Know who does what and where
Check ancillary gear is at the listed location

tip: Walk the ETB with the bosun once, using the real gear. Everyone then knows where each item is.

title: Anchoring operations
plain: Do officers know the company anchoring procedures, and do records show recent anchoring followed them?
why: Anchoring beyond equipment limits or in bad weather can damage the windlass or let the ship drag.
checks: Procedures and checklists covering anchorage choice, depth, weather limits, team and supervision
Records of a recent anchoring: checklists, windlass and brake checks, weather and depth
Windlass, anchors, chain and stoppers condition
Anchor brake adjustment: can you show how it is checked
Anchors free to use: chain not hard against stopper bar, lashings off in port
ready: Anchoring procedure and checklists
Recent anchoring records, Bridge Log Book and bell book
Windlass brake check record
Maximum anchorage depth marked on the windlass or posted on the bridge
traps: No procedure or checklists, or missing depth, weather, team or supervision limits
Anchored or stayed at anchor beyond company weather limits
Anchored in water deeper than the company limit
Maximum anchorage depth not marked or posted; pre and post anchoring checks not done
Windlass system defective, or officer cannot show how to verify brake adjustment
Chain resting on stopper bar in coastal waters or port, so anchor not free
say: Our procedure sets anchorage selection, depth and weather limits, team and supervision, and equipment checks before and after use. We complete the checklists each time. Anchors are kept free for emergency use, and I can show how we check the windlass brake setting.

practice.q: What is the maximum depth you can anchor in?
When would you leave the anchorage?
a: At the company weather limits in the procedure

tip: Put the max anchorage depth on the windlass and the bridge. It is a simple observation to avoid.

title: Mooring team supervision and composition
plain: Do officers and ratings know who supervises each mooring and anchoring station and how many people are needed?
why: Poor supervision and too few people on the mooring deck cause injuries and line failures.
checks: Company procedure on supervisors, team size and roles for mooring and anchoring
MSMP sections on manning and training and operations plans
Whether a deck officer and a rating can say who supervises each station
Toolbox talks or risk assessment review before the operation
Hours of rest records against the real team used
ready: Company procedure on team composition and supervision
MSMP manning and operations plan sections
Hours of rest for the previous full month
Training and competence records if a non-officer supervises
Risk assessments for recent operations if required
traps: MSMP does not state team size or supervision per station
Officer cannot find the procedure on who supervises each station
Officer or rating unfamiliar with team or supervision expectations
Hours of rest show the team was not as required
Rating supervises with no evidence of training and competence assessment
say: Our procedure names who supervises each mooring station and the minimum team for each type of operation. We hold a toolbox talk before the operation and keep communications tested. Hours of rest records match the team we used.

practice.q: Who supervises the forward station?
a: Name the role from the procedure

practice.q: How are the team briefed?
What must you be able to explain from the mooring plan?
a: Your station, its team and the supervisor
The layout and lead of each line

tip: If a rating may supervise a station, keep the training record handy. The inspector will ask for it.

title: Dangers of working around mooring lines
plain: Do deck officers and ratings know winch safe operation and the dangers around lines under tension?
why: Snap-back from a parted line and unsafe winch use are leading causes of deaths on mooring decks.
checks: Mooring procedure on safety during mooring and near tensioned lines
Winch drums out of gear with locking pins available
Control levers free, return to neutral and marked for heave and slack
No sign that controls were tied for unmanned use
Warning signs and barriers, safe access platforms
Interview: how were you told about snap-back
ready: Mooring procedure with supervisor and rating roles, hand signals, snap-back areas
Toolbox talk before every mooring
Clutch locking pins in place
Snap-back areas identified, warning signs and barriers in place
traps: No procedure on mooring safety; officer or rating does not know the procedure or snap-back danger
No toolbox talk before mooring
Stepping over a line under tension when another route exists; no warning signs or barriers
Drum left in gear while in service with brake on, or clutch pins missing
Levers stiff, not returning to neutral, not marked, or tied in heave or slack
Winch platforms damaged or with missing plates
say: We hold a toolbox talk before every mooring and use signs and barriers around snap-back areas. I know not to stand in the bight or step over a line under tension. Winch controls return to neutral, are marked, and clutches are locked with pins.

practice.q: Where is the snap-back danger zone?
a: Any area the procedure identifies as at risk if a line parts
Warning signs and barriers keep people clear

practice.q: What safety checks do you do on the winch before use?
a: Clutch engaged and locked, drum in or out of gear as required

tip: Never tie a control lever. If it is stiff, report and fix it before the next mooring.

title: STS operations checklists
plain: Were the right industry STS checklists used, and are full records of the operation kept?
why: STS checklists catch hazards unique to two ships together, such as mooring, fenders, hose and electrical isolation.
checks: Company procedure requiring OCIMF STS Guide checklists and record keeping
Current STS checklists, with a standard pre-transfer checklist and a vapour balancing checklist if used
Past STS records from the last twelve months or last six operations
That items ticked had the evidence
Checks and signatures from the other ship or terminal for in-port transfers
ready: STS procedure and checklists (at sea 1 to 5, in port 6 and 6A)
Joint Plan of Operation and service provider risk assessment
Mooring plan, fender and hose certificates, notification to coastal authority
Drill records, crew experience records, Master's post-operation feedback
traps: No procedure requiring the OCIMF checklists or keeping records
Wrong checklist set used, at sea for in port or the reverse
Checklist missing or not used, or items ticked with no evidence
Standard pre-transfer checklist not used with STS ones; no vapour balancing checklist when balancing
Repetitive checks not done, or checks not actually carried out on deck
Records for past operations incomplete, or second ship or terminal signatures missing
say: Our procedure requires the OCIMF STS checklists for the type of operation, together with the normal pre-transfer checklist. We complete them before, during and after the transfer, keep the full record file, and the other ship signs where required.

practice.q: Which checklists do you use for an at sea STS?
a: Pre-fixture, before operations, before run-in and mooring

practice.q: What records do you keep?
a: Mooring plan and fender or hose certificates
Notifications, drills, crew experience, Master feedback

tip: If the ship has never done STS and does not plan to, the guidance says to mark Not Answerable then Not Applicable. Be sure it is true.

title: STS Joint Plan of Operation (JPO)
plain: For at sea STS, is an accurate Joint Plan of Operation on board, known by officers, and followed?
why: The JPO makes sure both ships and the service provider agree how mooring, transfer and unmooring will be done safely.
checks: Company procedure requiring a JPO for every STS
JPO has all content from the OCIMF STS Guide for this operation
Risk assessment fits the location and the type of STS
How electrical arcing between the ships is prevented
Mandatory notifications made, mooring as agreed, environmental limits respected, unmooring sequence written
ready: Company procedure and the ship's STS Operations Plan
JPO from the service provider or POAC
Risk assessment for this location and operation
Evidence of notifications to authorities
Briefing record for officers and ratings
traps: No procedure requiring a JPO, or no JPO for the operation on board; JPO missing information required by the OCIMF guide
Officer does not know the JPO, or officer or rating not briefed before start
Risk assessment does not match the location or type of STS
JPO silent on arcing prevention, or measures not actually fitted
No evidence of mandatory notifications; not moored per JPO
Transfer continued after environmental limits were exceeded
say: Our procedure requires a JPO for every STS, and we review and brief it before starting. It covers mooring, transfer, environmental limits and unmooring, and how we prevent arcing between the ships. We moor as agreed and stop if limits are exceeded.

practice.q: How do you prevent sparks between the two ships?
a: Single insulating flange at one manifold or in each hose string
Or a single length of electrically discontinuous hose
Or hoses built to prevent static build-up

practice.q: When would you stop the transfer?
a: When environmental limits in the JPO are exceeded
Disconnect and unmoor as the JPO sequence says
Inform the other ship and POAC

tip: Brief the deck ratings on the JPO too. The inspector may interview a deck rating.

title: STS Operations Plan
plain: Are the Master, officers and deck ratings familiar with the ship's own STS Operations Plan?
why: A ship-specific plan makes sure STS mooring and cargo work is done the same, planned way each time.
checks: Plan on board, with copies on the bridge, cargo transfer station and engine room
For oil cargo (MARPOL Annex I): approved by the Administration
For other cargoes: in line with OCIMF STS Guide Annex A
Updated with mooring plan and cargo plan of the current operation
Officer and a rating who took part recently: where it is and what it says
ready: STS Operations Plan, current and complete
Copies in bridge, cargo control and engine room
Administration approval for oil cargoes
Current mooring and cargo plans added
Contingency plan, spill reporting and ESD and breakaway procedures in the plan
traps: No plan at all, even if the ship has never done STS
Oil cargo plan not approved by flag
Plan out of date or incomplete
A copy missing from bridge, cargo station or engine room
Officer unfamiliar with where the plan is or what it says
Rating who took part recently does not know the plan
say: Our STS Operations Plan is approved where required and copies are on the bridge, cargo control and engine room. It gives the steps for mooring, transfer, ESD, breakaway and spill reporting. We update it with the mooring and cargo plans for each operation.

practice.q: Where is the STS Operations Plan kept?
What does it cover?
a: Cargo and ballast transfer, hoses, topping off
Roles, ESD and breakaway, drip trays, spill reporting, contingency plan

tip: If STS is never done on this ship, the guidance says Not Answerable then Not Applicable. Otherwise the plan must exist even if no STS has happened.

title: Vapour hose arrangement for buoy moorings
plain: Are the vapour manifolds fitted for handling the vapour hose at buoy moorings?
why: Without the right fittings the vapour hose cannot be supported or hung off safely, and liquid can carry into the floating hose.
checks: Vapour manifold supported as strongly as cargo manifolds
Hose rails strong and the same along their length, extending beyond the vapour manifold, stopper plates at both ends
Closed chock at ship's side in line with the manifold
Cruciform bollard, and two deck pad-eyes for a 16-inch floating hose
SWL marked on securing fittings, and a low point drain on the vapour line
ready: Mooring arrangement plan showing deck fittings by the manifold
Fittings marked with SWL
Drain arrangement at the lowest point of the vapour line
traps: Vapour manifold not supported to same strength as cargo manifolds
Hose rails not extended, not uniform, or lacking stopper plates at both ends
Closed chocks, cruciform bollards or pad-eyes missing
Securing fittings not marked with SWL
No means to drain the vapour manifold, so liquid could reach the floating hose
say: Our vapour manifolds are built for buoy mooring work. Supports, hose rails, closed chock, cruciform bollard and pad-eyes are in place and marked with SWL. The vapour line has a drain at its lowest point.

practice.q: What fittings do you need at the vapour manifold for SPM work?
a: Closed chock in line with manifold

practice.q: Why a drain at the low point?
a: Stops liquid carrying into the floating hose

tip: Only applies if your vapour manifold is designed for single buoy use. Keep the mooring arrangement plan showing these fittings.

title: SPM mooring arrangements
plain: Do officers know the procedures for mooring at an SPM or F(P)SO, and does the HVPQ describe the bow fittings correctly?
why: A badly equipped or poorly maintained bow system can fail under load at an SPM or F(P)SO.
checks: Company procedure: preparation, safe mooring instructions, inspection and maintenance of bow stoppers
Independent authority certificates for bow stoppers, closed fairleads and their foundations
Bow stopper marked with SWL and serial number, fairlead SWL not less than stopper
Records of bow stopper inspection and maintenance
Bow arrangement matches what the HVPQ says, pick-up line route clear
ready: SPM or F(P)SO mooring procedure
Mooring arrangement plan
Class certificates for stoppers, fairleads and structure
Inspection and maintenance records for stoppers
Surveys of stoppers, fairleads and structure at least every five years
traps: No procedure with preparation, instructions and stopper maintenance
Officer unfamiliar with the procedure; bow arrangements not as described in the HVPQ
Missing certificate for stopper, fairlead or foundation; stopper not marked with SWL and serial number
Fairlead SWL below the stopper SWL; no stopper inspection records; obstruction near the pick-up line route
Winch stowage drum too small, or warping drum used for the pick-up line
Wedges between pin and tongue, or a Smit bracket used as a stopper
say: Our procedure covers preparation, mooring and inspection of the bow stoppers for SPM and F(P)SO. The stoppers and fairleads are certified, marked with SWL and inspected. What the HVPQ says matches what you see on the forecastle.

practice.q: What must the bow stopper have?
a: Certificate from independent authority such as Class
Permanent SWL and serial number marking

practice.q: How is the pick-up line handled?
a: Stowage drum, not the warping drum
Drum big enough, no obstructions on the line route

tip: Compare the HVPQ bow details with the actual forecastle before the inspection.

title: Shuttle tanker bow mooring system
plain: Do officers know how to operate, inspect, test and maintain the bow mooring system for offshore terminals, and is it in good condition?
why: The bow system takes huge hawser loads, and a failure or accidental chain release at an offshore terminal can be disastrous.
checks: Company procedure, possibly in field operations manuals and maintenance plan
Inspection, test and maintenance records, including chain stopper open and close time within 30 seconds
Fairlead, hardwood deck protection, chain stopper, traction winch and manual brake release
Rope pulling unit, service crane, hydraulic power pack, messenger line cutter
Your answers on preventing accidental chafe chain release, brake release on power failure, and the messenger cutter
ready: Procedure and Field Offloading Manual
Maintenance and test records
Chain stopper marked with SWL
Tension monitor for the hawser load
Evidence of chain stopper timing test
traps: No company procedure, or officer unfamiliar with chain release prevention, manual brake release or messenger cutter
Records missing or incomplete, no chain stopper timing test within 30 seconds
Stopper not marked with SWL; fairlead not stainless steel or spark free cladding missing
Hardwood protection (75 mm) missing or damaged, or recess bolts without hardwood plugs; no hawser tension monitor
Manual brake release not in a safe place, winch parts or brakes unprotected, rope pulling unit without guards
Operator's view of the rope stowing area blocked
say: Our procedure covers operation, inspection, testing and maintenance of the bow mooring system. We guard against accidental chain release, and I know the manual brake release and the messenger line cutter. Records show the chain stopper operates within 30 seconds.

practice.q: What if the traction winch loses power?
a: Located in a safe area away from debris

practice.q: What if the messenger line goes toward the thruster or propeller?
a: Cut the line to avoid fouling
Know where the cutter is and who uses it

tip: Only for shuttle tankers with bow loading systems. Time the chain stopper and write it down.

title: Chief Engineer's standing and daily orders
plain: Has the Chief Engineer written standing orders and daily orders, and have all engineers signed them?
why: Clear orders make every watchkeeper know what the company and the Chief expect in the engine room.
checks: Company procedure requiring standing and daily orders
Current standing orders signed and dated by CE and all engineers
Daily order book entries dated, timed and signed by CE and each watch officer
Engine room log book showing the daily orders were followed
Your knowledge of the orders
ready: Company procedure on writing orders
Standing orders, signed and dated by CE at takeover and by all engineers
Daily order book
Engine room log book and records for machinery mode changes
traps: No company procedure requiring orders; engineer cannot explain the orders
CE's own standing orders not written, signed and dated
Engineers on board have not signed (unless joined that day); orders conflict with company procedures
Standing orders missing UMS entry, alarm response, defect action, transfers, incinerator, hot and cold work
Daily orders not signed, dated and timed, or watch engineers not signed
Log shows orders not followed
say: I write standing orders to support the SMS and the daily orders for each day's operation. Every engineer signs, and the watch engineers sign the daily orders before taking over. The orders cover UMS entry, alarms, defects, transfers, incinerator and hot work.

practice.q: What do the standing orders say about alarms?
a: Actions on alarm, especially critical equipment

practice.q: What goes into daily orders?
a: Timing of engine room status change and tests for manoeuvring
When incinerator or OWS may be used

tip: Daily orders are not generally needed for days in open ocean with UMS. Do write them for port, manoeuvring and changes.

title: Testing propulsion, steering, thrusters and power plant
plain: Do engineers know the tests before arrival and departure, and are checklists and log entries completed?
why: Failure of propulsion or steering during manoeuvring can cause collision, grounding or a spill.
checks: Company procedure listing what is tested, when, by whom and how it is recorded
Recent pre-arrival and pre-departure checklists and log entries
Whether you understand any test on the checklist you are asked
Local operation of the steering gear shown by the engineer
Defects found during tests reported to bridge and in the defect system
ready: Procedure and checklists matching the equipment fitted
Completed pre-arrival, pre-departure and pre-transit checklists
Engine log book entries, printer and data logger records
Defect reports for items found faulty in tests
traps: No documented procedure for tests at defined points
Engineer does not know a test on the checklist
Engineer cannot operate the steering gear locally
Checklists not matching the equipment fitted
Tests not done or not recorded
Defects found in testing not repaired or not reported
say: Our procedure and checklists define the tests before arrival, departure and transit, who does them and how they are recorded. Steering gear is checked and tested within 12 hours before departure, and our checklists cover main engine, generators and the other items. Any defect goes to the bridge and into the defect system.

practice.q: What do you test before departure?
a: Standby generator, emergency batteries, communications and alarms

practice.q: Can you show local steering gear control?
a: Operate the steering from the steering gear room

tip: Practise local steering operation with the 3/E until it is automatic. It is a common request.
refs: ICS Engine Room Procedures Guide Annex A

title: Periodic machinery space rounds (non-UMS)
plain: Do engineers know the company procedure for engine room rounds, and do logs and checklists show rounds were done?
why: Regular rounds catch leaks, noises and temperatures early, before they become breakdowns or fires.
checks: Company procedure for routine engine room rounds
Vessel-specific round checklists covering all spaces and main machinery
Checklists and logs showing rounds were made as required
Local readings recorded against remote values
Your knowledge of an item you are asked about
ready: Procedure and ship-specific round checklists
Completed checklists and log book entries
Operational records for recent voyages
traps: No procedure requiring periodic rounds
Engineer does not know a check on the list
No ship-specific round checklists
Rounds not done as the procedure requires
say: Our procedure requires regular rounds by the watch engineer with a checklist for our machinery. I record local readings and compare them with the remote values, and report any abnormality to the Chief Engineer.

practice.q: Take any item on the round sheet. What do you check?
a: What to look at, hear, smell or feel

practice.q: Why compare local and remote readings?

tip: This question is for ships without a UMS notation. Make sure the checklist covers every space and the main machinery.
refs: ICS Engine Room Procedures Guide 8.5 and 8.9.3

title: Machinery space rounds, manned and UMS
plain: Do engineers know the rounds and monitoring procedure for both manned and unmanned (UMS) periods, with records to prove it?
why: Running unattended without the right checks and safeguards is how engine room fires and floods go unnoticed.
checks: Company procedure for manned rounds and checks before UMS
Pre-UMS checklist covering all SOLAS II-1 Part E systems
Maximum UMS period allowed by class or flag
Logs, checklists and alarm records for recent voyages
Your knowledge of an item on the checklist
ready: Procedure with manned and UMS round checklists
Completed checklists and engine log book
Alarm records for recent voyages
Evidence UMS equipment tested and working
Defect report for any reliability concern
traps: No procedure for rounds in manned periods and before UMS
No ship-specific checklists; engineer does not know the purpose of a check
Rounds not carried out as procedure says
UMS longer than allowed by company or class; UMS used when procedure required manned
Manned on open sea for reliability but cause not in the defect system
UMS with Part E equipment out of service or defective
say: Our procedure requires rounds in manned mode and a full round with checklist before going UMS. The checklist covers the systems required by SOLAS II-1 Part E. We respect the maximum UMS period and record any reliability reason for going manned.

practice.q: What do you do before leaving the engine room unmanned?
a: Complete round with the pre-UMS checklist
Check alarms, safety and fire systems work
Hand over to duty engineer and bridge informed

practice.q: When would the procedure make you manned?

tip: If you go manned because of a reliability worry, put the cause on a defect report so the shore side can fix it.

title: Local control of propulsion machinery
plain: Do engineers know how to operate, inspect and test local control of propulsion machinery if the remote control fails?
why: If remote control fails during manoeuvring, you must take control locally fast to keep the ship safe.
checks: Company procedure: actions on remote control failure, how often local control is inspected and tested
Manual controls or HMIs at local stations and instructions posted nearby
Inspection and test records, in the planned maintenance system if needed
Communication with the bridge at each local control station
For CPP: failure mode known by engineers and navigation officers, with a notice posted
ready: Procedure for local control operation, inspection and testing
Ship-specific operating instructions posted at each local control station
Test records and planned maintenance entries
Working communication to the bridge from each station
CPP failure mode notice on bridge and in machinery space, if fitted
traps: No company procedure; engineer does not know purpose, operation or testing of local control
Instructions not posted near the controls
Local control not in the planned maintenance system, or records incomplete
Maintenance records say done but local station shows it was not
Communication from a local station not ready or defective
No CPP failure mode notice, or navigation officer does not know the mode; local control systems defective
say: Our procedure covers what to do if remote control fails, and how often we inspect and test local control. Ship-specific instructions are posted at each station and we have communications with the bridge. I can demonstrate operation and testing.

practice.q: The bridge remote control fails during manoeuvring. What do you do?
a: Go to local control as the posted instructions say
Follow company procedure and report the defect

practice.q: What is the CPP failure mode on this ship?
a: State it (full ahead, full astern or zero pitch)
Notice posted on bridge and in machinery space

tip: Run a local control drill with the 3/E and a bridge call. It also proves the communication works.

title: Emergency generator
plain: Do officers know how to start the emergency generator, and do records prove it is tested as required?
why: In a blackout the emergency generator keeps essential services running, so it must start every time.
checks: Company procedure with starting, supply to switchboard, fuel system, testing and frequency
Starting instructions posted at the generator, clear for non-engineers
Auto start and supply to emergency switchboard; witnessing start by primary and secondary means
Voltage and frequency on the emergency switchboard, fuel level, quick closing valve, fire-flaps
Test records on load, with consumers loaded, spare starter motor tested
ready: Company procedure and ship-specific start procedure
Posted starting instructions
Test records for generator, quick closing valve and spare starter motor
Fuel quantity for 18 hours marked on the tank gauge
Insulation mats in front of and behind the emergency switchboard
traps: No company procedure, or not set to start automatically; no posted instructions, or unclear instructions
Officers not familiar with starting and connecting to the switchboard; does not start within three attempts by primary or secondary means
Voltage or frequency out of limits; no spare starter motor where needed, or not tested
Tests or records missing, no on-load run, consumers not loaded
Fuel not enough for 18 hours or level not marked; fuel not suitable for sub-zero trading
Quick closing valve faulty, closed or hard to reach, fire-flaps do not operate; insulation mats missing, exhaust piping wasted
say: Our procedure covers primary and secondary starting, supply to the emergency switchboard, on-load testing and the fuel quick closing valve. Instructions are posted at the generator and all officers know them. Test records are available, with on-load runs and consumers checked.

practice.q: Show me how to start the emergency generator.
a: Connect to the emergency switchboard if not automatic

practice.q: How much fuel must you have?
a: Enough for full load for at least 18 hours
Minimum level marked on the gauge
Sub-zero grade if trading in cold

tip: Deck officers can be interviewed too. Make sure they have read the start instructions. On-load test is not done during an inspection.

title: Battery emergency source of power
plain: Do engineers know how emergency batteries are inspected, maintained and tested, and are the batteries charged and in good condition?
why: If the emergency source is batteries, they must carry the emergency load when main power fails.
checks: Company procedure: inspection, condition assessment, testing and retirement criteria
Records of inspections, voltage and specific gravity, blackout simulation test, installation date
Battery compartment: clean, terminals protected, vents clear, no storage
Batteries fully charged and charger working
Your knowledge of the blackout simulation test
ready: Procedure with retirement criteria based on age or condition
Inspection and condition records
Records of test bringing the battery system on load in a blackout simulation
Battery installation date
Maker's instructions for sealed, gel or NiFe batteries in the space
traps: No procedure, or no retirement criteria; officer unfamiliar with procedure or blackout simulation test
No records of inspection, maintenance or tests
Voltage or specific gravity records show poor condition
Batteries not replaced per retirement criteria or in poor physical state
Exposed terminals without caps; battery locker used for storage
Batteries not fully charged, charger defective
say: Our procedure covers regular inspection, voltage and specific gravity checks, and the full system test on load in a blackout simulation. We keep records, know the retirement criteria and the battery installation date. Terminals are protected and the locker is kept clear.

practice.q: How do you judge the condition of a battery?
a: Check electrolyte level, cleanliness, terminals, vents

practice.q: How long must the emergency batteries last?
a: Supply the designed load for up to 18 hours

tip: Only applies if emergency power is batteries. Check the terminal caps and make sure nothing is stored in the locker.

title: Exhaust gas cleaning system (EGCS)
plain: Do engineers know how to operate, calibrate and maintain the scrubber safely and follow regulations?
why: Scrubbers involve hazardous chemicals, gases and wash water, and non-compliance means breaking MARPOL or local rules.
checks: Company procedure and risk assessments: hazards, training, PPE, signage, routine operation, calibration, failure actions, records
Required documents: SOx Emissions Compliance Plan, Technical Manual, Onboard Monitoring Manual, EGCS Record Book
You describing routine operation and failure actions
How to close the EGCS overboard valve in an emergency
Waste and chemical handling, planned maintenance records, training records
ready: Procedure and risk assessments
SOx Emissions Compliance Plan, Technical Manual, Onboard Monitoring Manual
EGCS Record Book or electronic log, kept current
Planned maintenance and calibration records
Training or familiarisation records
Notification record to authorities if the system failed
traps: No procedure or no risk assessment; officer does not know routine operation or how to shut the overboard valve
Used where company procedure or local rules prohibit it; waste, sludge or washwater not managed as required
Chemicals or calibration gases not stored per procedure
No training or familiarisation evidence; required document missing from board
Maintenance and calibration not in planned maintenance or not done; record book not maintained
System defective without notification to authorities per MEPC.1/Circ.883
say: We have a procedure and risk assessments covering hazards, PPE, training, routine operation, calibration and failures. The required documents and the record book are on board and current. I know how to close the overboard valve in an emergency.

practice.q: What if the scrubber fails or goes out of compliance?
a: Follow the failure procedure and MEPC.1/Circ.883
Record start time, actions and resolution in the EGCS record book
Change to compliant fuel if not back in compliance within one hour
Report a failure over one hour, or repeated failures, to flag and port State

practice.q: What goes into the EGCS record book?
a: Start and stop of each unit

tip: Only for ships with a scrubber. Know where the overboard valve is and how to close it.

title: Seawater pipelines, sea chests and pumps
plain: Are seawater pipes, sea chests and pumps in good condition and free of temporary repairs?
why: A weak seawater system can fail and flood the machinery space.
checks: Seawater pipes, sea chests, storm valves, hull penetrations and pumps
Corrosion, pitting, hard rust, leaks, wasted pipe in way of clips
Bellows deformed, clips or supports missing or heavily corroded
Any temporary repairs, doublers, patent couplings, flexible hoses used as replacement
Class approval for completed repairs
ready: Machinery space pipeline drawings and specifications
Class approval for any permanent repair
Planned maintenance on seawater system
Clips and supports refitted after any repair
traps: Corroded piping with pitting or hard rust
Leaks on pipes, valves or pumps; deformed bellows
Pipe thinned at clips and supports, or clips missing
Temporary repair such as clamp or bandage
Unacceptable permanent repair such as welded doubler or coupling
No class approval for a pipe repair; flexible hose used instead of a failed metal pipe
say: We inspect the seawater system regularly, including outboard of ship-side valves, bends, clips, bellows and wet areas. Any local repair is treated as temporary until it is replaced by class approved pipe. We have no temporary repairs now.

practice.q: Where do you look for weak points in seawater pipes?
a: Outboard of ship-side valves, bends and elbows
Bellows and wet or hidden areas

practice.q: What is acceptable as a permanent repair?
a: Replace the length of pipe with class approved material
Examined and approved by class surveyor
Patent couplings only if part of original design

tip: Look in the hidden corners behind pumps and under plates. Inspectors do.

title: Bilge monitoring devices
plain: Do officers know how bilge level devices and alarms are tested, and do records prove the tests were done?
why: Bilge alarms give the first warning of flooding in the engine room, pumproom or thruster space.
checks: Procedure requiring all bilge level and flooding devices and alarms to be identified and tested
Test records including any activation delay
Alarm test during the tour: right places, delay as designed
Any device or alarm modified or inhibited
Protection of cargo pumproom, ballast pumproom, main machinery space and bow thruster space
ready: Company procedure and list of every bilge alarm fitted
Test records for each device, delay and alarm
Planned maintenance job instructions for bilge alarms
For OBO: alarms in forward ballast tanks and dry or void spaces forward of the foremost hold
traps: No procedure for testing all level devices
Officer not familiar with the procedure in own area
No records of testing, including delay
Device or alarm defective
Alarm modified or stopped from activating
One of the required spaces with no bilge level monitor
say: We identified every bilge and water level alarm on the ship and test each one with its activation delay under our procedure. The alarms activate at the places required. Records are available and nothing is inhibited.

practice.q: Which spaces need a bilge alarm?
a: OBO: forward ballast tanks and dry spaces

practice.q: What do you check in a test?
a: Remote alarm in the required locations

tip: Test and log pumproom and bow thruster space alarms too, not only the engine room. Check where the alarm repeats on the bridge and CCR.

title: Emergency compressed air starting system
plain: Do engineers know how to operate, inspect and test the emergency air compressor and reservoir, and are they in good condition?
why: After a dead ship condition, the emergency air system must restart the machinery without outside help.
checks: Procedure for operating, inspecting and testing the emergency compressor and reservoir
Procedure for using them to bring machinery back from dead ship
Test and inspection records
Compressor condition and reservoir at required pressure
You explaining how to use them to start a generator engine
ready: Company procedures for operation, testing and dead ship use
Regular inspection and test records
Emergency reservoir at required pressure
Compressor regularly tested to the generator starting pressure
Power source known (hand-started diesel or electric from emergency source)
traps: No procedures for operation, testing or dead ship use
Officer not familiar with the procedure or with starting a generator from it
No records, or tests not as per procedure
Reservoir not at required pressure
Emergency compressor defective
say: Our procedure covers operating and testing the emergency air compressor and keeping the reservoir at pressure. I know how to use them to start a generator from dead ship. Test records are available.

practice.q: How do you restart from a dead ship?
a: Restore power and then machinery per procedure

practice.q: How is the emergency compressor driven?
a: Hand-started diesel engine or electric motor
If electric, from the emergency source

tip: Run the compressor to generator starting pressure at each test and write down the time and pressure.
